title: The market-fall playbook
objectives: Explain why a falling NAV helps a SIP.
body_md:
A distributor's biggest contribution to client returns often comes in a market fall: keeping the client invested when instinct says sell.

## Market-fall playbook

- Call first. When markets fall sharply, contact clients before they call in panic, starting with recent and first-time investors.
- Reconnect to the goal. Show goal progress and horizon, not the day's loss.
- Explain the SIP advantage. Lower prices mean more units for the same instalment.
- Use history, without promises. Past falls and recoveries show that volatility is normal; never promise when or whether markets will recover.
- Act only if the plan says so. Rebalance by rule, or deploy planned STP money; never make emotional switches.
- Record the conversation and follow up in writing.
example: The Nifty falls 15% in a month. A SIP of ₹10,000 buys 500 units at a NAV of ₹20 before the fall and 625 units at ₹16 after it. You call recent investors first and show them the extra units.
say: Markets have fallen, and your SIP is now buying more units at lower prices. Stopping now would lock in the worst part of the cycle.
Falls like this have happened before. Let's look at your goal and horizon.
never: Markets will recover soon, I promise.
Sell now and come back later.

talk_track.title: March 2020: the test every investor faced
talk_track.text: Every distributor remembers March 2020. The Nifty 50 fell close to 40% in about a month, closing at 7,610 on 23rd March. Phones rang non-stop, and many clients wanted to stop their SIPs or redeem everything. Yet less than a year later, by February 2021, the index had nearly doubled from that low. Clients who stopped or redeemed at the bottom locked in their losses and missed the rebound. Clients whose distributors called them early and kept them invested came out ahead. We can't promise any future fall will recover the same way, but this is exactly the moment where our value shows.

talk_track.title: The investor emotion cycle
talk_track.text: This is the investor emotion cycle, and every client goes around it. As markets rise, optimism turns to excitement, and at the very top, euphoria. That is when most investors pile in, exactly when risk is highest. Then the market turns: anxiety, fear, panic, and at the bottom, despondency. That is when most investors sell, often just before the recovery begins with hope and optimism again. Our job is to move clients against their own emotions: calm at the peak, steady at the bottom. When a client tells you how they feel, you can usually place them on this curve.

talk_track.title: A falling NAV buys more units
talk_track.text: Here's how to explain the SIP advantage in a fall. Take a ₹10,000 monthly SIP over twelve hypothetical months. The NAV falls from 100 to 70, then recovers to 108. Look at the bars: as the NAV falls, the same ₹10,000 buys more units, peaking at 143 units when the NAV is 70. Because of this, the average cost per unit is ₹85.6, lower than the average NAV of ₹87.3. And the result: ₹1.2 lakh invested is worth about ₹1.51 lakh, even though the NAV ended only 8% above where it started. The months that felt worst did the most work. That's why stopping a SIP in a fall is the costliest mistake.

talk_track.title: The market-fall playbook
talk_track.text: Stage five, Navigate behaviour, is where a distributor earns trust for life. When markets fall sharply, follow six steps. One, call first, before clients call you in panic, starting with recent and first-time investors. Two, reconnect them to their goal and horizon, not today's loss. Three, explain that their SIP is now buying more units at lower prices. Four, use history to show falls are normal, but never promise when or whether markets will recover. Five, act only if the plan says so: rebalance by rule, never make emotional switches. Six, record the conversation and follow up in writing.

check.q: When the NAV falls, what happens to a running SIP?

check.why: Lower prices mean more units, which lowers the average cost per unit.

check.q: Which statement is acceptable to a client during a market fall?
o: "Let's move into this new NFO instead."
"Falls like this have happened before; let's look at your goal and horizon."
check.why: Use history without promises. Never assure returns, capital protection or recovery timelines.
